title: Consensus and controversy of liquid biopsy using circulating tumour DNA (ctDNA) for molecular residual disease detection in colorectal cancer
abstract: Circulating tumour DNA (ctDNA) detection after curative-intent treatment is one of the strongest prognostic biomarkers in colorectal cancer (CRC), but its clinical utility remains incompletely established. Randomised trials have shown that ctDNA-informed management can reduce adjuvant chemotherapy exposure in selected stage II colon cancer, yet non-inferiority was not established in stage III disease, and cytotoxic escalation for ctDNA-positive molecular residual disease (MRD) has not improved recurrence-free survival. These mixed interventional results do not diminish the prognostic validity of ctDNA, but suggest that its clinical utility depends on four interacting considerations: the biological state represented by ctDNA positivity, the timing of testing and intervention, assay and sampling heterogeneity, and trial design. Serial ctDNA dynamics may provide additional biological and prognostic information, as sustained clearance, transient clearance, persistence, and re-emergence are unlikely to represent equivalent states of MRD. Western Pacific studies have led the field, including GALAXY and ALTAIR in Japan and Taiwan, DYNAMIC in Australia, FIND and CINTS-R in China, and CLAUDIA in Korea. However, regional implementation is constrained by uneven laboratory infrastructure, cost, regulatory access, and limited evidence from Southeast Asia and Pacific lower-resource settings. Outside clinical trials, ctDNA should refine prognosis rather than dictate omission, intensification, or initiation of treatment. Future trials should align assay performance, biological timing, and intervention mechanism, and use patient-centred endpoints capable of demonstrating that acting on ctDNA improves outcomes.

title: Postpartum risk and prognosis of pregnancy-associated intracerebral haemorrhage: a nationwide cohort-crossover study
abstract: Background The temporal pattern and maternal-offspring burden of pregnancy-associated intracerebral haemorrhage (P–ICH), an uncommon but devastating pregnancy-postpartum complication, have not been comprehensively elucidated. Methods This cohort-crossover study linked four nationwide databases to include pregnancies from 2012 to 2020 in Taiwan. Incidence rate ratios (IRRs) for P–ICH were estimated across six intervals from pregnancy through the full 1-year postpartum, with the corresponding period 730 days prior serving as the control. Cohort-time-control and cohort-cohort-time-control sensitivity analyses were performed to adjust for the 730-day age gap. Maternal-offspring outcomes were compared between pregnancies with and without P–ICH. Findings 406 P–ICH events were identified (crude incidence 19·22 per 100,000 pregnancies). The overall IRR was 1·79 (95% CI 1·52–2·10). The P–ICH risk showed no meaningful difference across pregnancy but peaked during 0–42 days postpartum (IRR 7·44; 95% CI 4·55–12·18), remaining elevated through 43–180 days (IRR 1·58; 95% CI 1·13–2·20) and 181–365 days (IRR 1·38; 95% CI 1·04–1·83) postpartum. Postpartum elevations were sustained meaningfully in sensitivity analyses, except the 181–365-day cohort-time-control estimate. Women with HDP other than chronic hypertension showed a greater P–ICH risk than those without (p interaction = 0·0024). Two-year maternal (12·1% vs 0·1%) and offspring (2·2% vs 0·4%) mortality were substantially higher following P–ICH, with 38·8% of maternal deaths in women developing P–ICH 43–365 days postpartum. Interpretation P–ICH imposes a substantial and extended postpartum burden, supporting at least 6-month postpartum surveillance and prevention. Funding National Cheng Kung University Hospital.

title: Accelerating the Western Pacific tobacco endgame
authors: The Lancet Regional Health – Western Pacific
abstract: Tobacco control was one of the key themes at this year's World Cancer Congress in September 2026, in Hong Kong, China. Discussions were centred on innovative tobacco cessation and control measures, new nicotine products, and industry interference. These issues are particularly relevant to the Western Pacific region, which has the largest population of tobacco users, but the slowest rate of reduction in tobacco use among all WHO regions.
